active_learning.evidence: Student does most of the work answering questions and computing, e.g., turns 19, 28, 30, 44; tutor explanations are brief.

direct_instruction_active_practice.evidence: Each teaching segment is followed by a question (e.g., turns 5→6, 14→15), though sometimes tutor stacks two tutor turns (14+15, 22+23).

deliberate_practice.evidence: Problems are calibrated but corrective feedback is undermined by tutor arithmetic errors (turn 31: '360-190=170', turn 38: '180-140=40', turn 22: '360-100-110=150').

mastery_learning.evidence: Tutor declares mastery prematurely at turn 31 ('You've mastered the method') despite confirming a wrong arithmetic result.

cognitive_load.evidence: One idea at a time generally; turn 32 abruptly introduces angles-on-a-line without a worked example, increasing load.

layering.evidence: Turn 38 explicitly links the two rules (360° around point vs 180° on a line), connecting new to prior.

non_interference.evidence: Angles-on-a-line introduced immediately after angles-around-a-point (turn 32), then mixed at turn 40, causing the exact confusion the principle warns about.

interleaving.evidence: Some variation (2 angles, 3 angles, MCQ, straight line), but mixing happens before mastery is consolidated, creating confusion not productive interleaving.

testing_effect.evidence: Student attempts retrieval before hints (turns 7, 26, 28); tutor doesn't over-hint initially.

targeted_remediation.evidence: After repeated wrong answers (turns 9, 11) tutor recycles the same MCQ rather than diagnosing the prereq; arithmetic errors are never remediated because tutor itself states wrong sums.

strongest_behaviors: Consistent return to retrieval questions after each explanation, keeping the student active
Explicit contrast between the two angle rules at turn 41 ('straight line sum to 180°... around a point sum to 360°')
weakest_behaviors: Tutor produces multiple arithmetic errors while confirming student work (turns 22, 31, 38), corrupting feedback
No targeted remediation on the underlying arithmetic/subtraction bottleneck; tutor instead falsely affirms wrong sums

prompt_recommendations.title: Mandate arithmetic verification before confirming student answers
prompt_recommendations.rationale: The tutor repeatedly confirms incorrect arithmetic, e.g., '360° - 100° - 110° = 150°' and '360° - 190° = 170°', undermining the entire lesson.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Before writing any '= <number>' in a response, internally recompute the arithmetic step-by-step. If the student's stated result disagrees with your recomputation, state the correct value and treat the student answer as incorrect. Never write 'Exactly right' next to a number you have not just verified.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Eliminates arithmetic contradictions and false-positive affirmations.

prompt_recommendations.title: Forbid premature mastery declarations
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Tutor says 'You've mastered the method' immediately after an arithmetic error, signaling mastery on a wrong answer.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Exactly! x = 360° - 190° = 170°. You've mastered the method
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Only use mastery language ('you've mastered', 'you've got it') after at least two consecutive fully correct problems with correct arithmetic, verified by you.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents false mastery signals and keeps practice going until real mastery.

prompt_recommendations.title: Diagnose prereq on repeated failure instead of re-asking the same MCQ
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After two wrong MCQ attempts (180°, 270°), the tutor offers the same four options again rather than diagnosing the conceptual bottleneck.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: One more try: A) 270° B) 180° C) 450° D) 360°
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: If a student answers the same MCQ incorrectly twice, do not re-present the same options. Instead, switch to a diagnostic open question targeting the prerequisite concept (e.g., 'How many degrees in a full turn?') before returning to the MCQ.

prompt_recommendations.title: Separate confusable topics with explicit signaling
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Angles-on-a-line is introduced abruptly right after angles-around-a-point, and the student then mixes the rules (turn 40).
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: okay! so if i have a straight line and one angle is 70 degrees, the other angle is 360 minus 70.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Do not introduce angles-on-a-straight-line in the same micro-session as angles-around-a-point until the student has solved 3 consecutive around-a-point problems correctly. When you do introduce it, explicitly contrast the two rules in a side-by-side worked example before practice.

prompt_recommendations.title: Respect single-question-per-turn and don't post two tutor turns back-to-back
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Tutor often emits an explanation turn followed immediately by a separate question turn (e.g., 14+15, 22+23, 38+39), fragmenting flow.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Now try this one: / Three angles around a point are 80°, 110°, and x°.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Each tutor message must end with exactly one question. Do not emit a follow-up tutor message before the student responds.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Cleaner turn structure; no truncated/duplicated tutor outputs.

prompt_recommendations.title: Handle student-authored problems with a brief redirect, not silent override
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Student tries to author problems (turns 16, 33) and tutor's redirect works, but later 'authoring_violation' flags suggest inconsistency; codify the rule.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: I see you want to practice with angles around a point — that's great! But let me stick with the problem I just posed
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: When the student proposes a problem, briefly acknowledge, then explicitly say you'll first finish the current problem and may use theirs afterward. Never silently abandon the current problem.

flow_recommendations.title: Add an arithmetic-check tool call before affirming numeric answers
flow_recommendations.rationale: Multiple arithmetic mistakes in tutor outputs are not caught by any verification step.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Catches arithmetic errors before they reach the student.

flow_recommendations.title: Failure-streak router to prerequisite practice
flow_recommendations.rationale: After three consecutive wrong MCQ answers about the 360° rule, the engine kept presenting the same item instead of routing to prereq drill.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Targeted remediation triggered automatically on failure streaks.

flow_recommendations.title: Mastery-gated topic transitions
flow_recommendations.rationale: Engine switched to straight-line angles (turn 32) immediately after one correct around-a-point answer that contained an arithmetic error.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: One angle on a straight line is 140°.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents topic switches before mastery is demonstrated.

experience_recommendations.title: Use consistent encouragement tone without overclaiming
experience_recommendations.rationale: Phrases like 'Exactly right!' attached to wrong arithmetic erode trust.
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Builds student trust by matching praise to actual correctness.

experience_recommendations.title: Inline the diagram or describe it when referenced
experience_recommendations.rationale: Tutor references a diagram with 8 rays the student cannot see, causing potential confusion.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: Looking at the diagram, you can see how this works — the point at the center has 8 rays

overall_summary: The session covers the correct concept and keeps the student actively answering, but is seriously undermined by repeated tutor arithmetic errors (150, 170, 40 instead of 150→150, 170→170, 40→40 — all wrong), premature mastery claims, and inadequate remediation when the student cycles through wrong MCQ answers. Topic separation between 'angles around a point' and 'angles on a line' is also too abrupt, causing the student to mix the two rules. Highest-priority fixes: verify all arithmetic before affirming, gate mastery language on verified correctness, and route repeated failures to prerequisite practice rather than recycling the same item.

bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: 180 degrees would be the sum of angles on a straight line... Try again

bea_evaluations.rationale: Pinpoints the missing 360°, gives corrected equation, asks for solution.

bea_evaluations.rationale: Tutor affirms as correct while silently substituting 170; doesn't tell student their 160 was wrong, no guidance, no next action on the error.

bea_evaluations.skip_reason: Student proposed a new problem rather than making a content mistake.

bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Not quite — let's double-check that calculation. 180° - 140° = ? Take your time

bea_evaluations.mistake_description: Student applied 360° rule to a straight-line problem (and invented one).
bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: be careful which rule you're using! For angles on a straight line, they sum to 180°... So if one angle on a straight line is 70°, the other angle is 180° - 70° = 110°.
bea_evaluations.rationale: Explicitly contrasts the two rules and corrects the calculation, then redirects to the MCQ.

bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: let's work through this step by step... First, what do 80° + 80° equal?
bea_evaluations.rationale: Scaffolds correctly but doesn't explicitly tell student why 380° is impossible (must be < 360°).

bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Not quite — let's check that subtraction carefully. 360° - 160° = ? Think of it as 360 - 160.
bea_evaluations.rationale: Identifies and locates the arithmetic error, prompts retry, but doesn't model subtraction strategy (e.g., 360-160 = 360-100-60).
